items.title: 12.10 Most of the matter in the observable universe is plasma

source_refs.note: Topic 12.10 (PDF 274-275, printed 271-272). The book's breakdown of the known 5% (68% hydrogen, 27% helium, 5% ordinary matter) repeats the dark-energy and dark-matter percentages and differs from 12.9; recorded for review.

blocks.text: Our universe is vaster than our thinking: we know about only some 5% of it and still do not know about the remaining 95%. For example, our universe consists of about 27% unknown matter called dark matter and about 68% of a mysterious antigravity material known as dark energy. Adding 27% and 68% gives 95%: we know nothing about 95% of the universe.

On the other hand, the book says that the 5% of the universe we know about consists of 68% hydrogen, 27% helium and 5% ordinary matter, and that hydrogen and helium are almost entirely in the plasma state. From these figures it concludes that 95% of the 5% of the observable universe is in the plasma state, while the remaining 5% is in the form of matter; hence most of the matter in the observable universe is plasma, since stars, which hold most visible matter, are made of hot ionized gas.

blocks.caption: The book's picture of the universe
rows: about 5%; mostly hydrogen and helium in the plasma state

blocks.prompt: Why can most of the matter in the observable universe be described as plasma?
blocks.explanation: Most visible matter is in stars and in hot gas between stars and galaxies. Their hydrogen and helium are so hot that their atoms are ionized into free electrons and nuclei, which is the plasma state; ordinary solids, liquids and neutral gases, like those on the Earth, are a very small fraction.

items: About 95% of the universe is unknown: dark matter (about 27%) and dark energy (about 68%). Of the known 5%, the hydrogen and helium are almost all ionized plasma, so most of the observable matter is plasma.
